chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Hawkins and Harrison's prank: Red Allen calls the wrong number home
summary: On Red's first road trip, Hawk and Jimmy Harrison teased him about his wife; he phoned home from the break, dialed the wrong number, played badly for days and gave notice until learning the mistake.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: The crew -- the heckling crew -- Hawk Coleman Hawkins, Jimmy Harrison, Buster Bailey and whatnot I remember one time -- Red was quite a family man, and he had a wife and had another little son that later became a trumpet player. Red's son.

Well anyway, one night the trombone player, Jimmy Harrison, asked Hawk around about midnight up on the bandstand -- I think they were in Nebraska -- Omaha, or Des Moines, or somewhere. -- Harrison said, "Hawk, what time do you think it is in New York now?" And then he'd tell him. He said to Red, "where do you think Gertie is now?" Gertie was Hawk's wife. And Jimmy Harrison's wife was named Kitty. He said, "Well, oh, I think Gertie and Kitty are around in the neighborhood bar." Now they were just sitting up talking, you know, you know they are not home, they're drinking, having fun. Red would act like he wouldn't hear it, you know. It began to get to him, you know. They'd say other things, you know.

So when Fletcher took intermission, the guys peeped to see where Red was going, you know. So Red went to the telephone and put a dime in to call New York, call his house. Huh. He was so nervous. Well, I'm ahead of myself. The operator -- he gave the number to call, and she rang it about three or four minutes. She said, "I'm sorry, they don't answer." He says, "What?" (Laughter) "Try again. I know my wife's home. I know this, and so she tried again. She says, "I'm sorry, sir, she's not there." Well, it turned out that he was so nervous, he had called the wrong number. He called the number of some corporation that's, naturally, closed at night.

So he came back up on the bandstand, and he's perturbed, man, and Red was usually a trumpet player that was just the opposite of Rex Stewart. He didn't play high. He played in the ligitimate range of the horn. So when he had a B flat, it sounded like an F, you know, because he stayed down in the range of the trumpet horn, and he could play. And he never missed because he was sure. He was very sure. He never, never, seldom hit a blue note.

Well, after this phone call that he made to New York and there was no answer, he came back on the bandstand, and he missed so much that everybody in the bandstand knew that he was missing and they knew why. Oh, they got a kick out of this.

And they didn't tell him any different on this for about four or five days, man, and this guy was sick, so much so that at the end of the night he went to Fletcher and told Fletcher that he was giving in his notice, two weeks' notice, that he had to go home, that somebody in ill. his family was the only thing. He wasn't playing right, one of those things, and it bothered Fletcher because he. -- before that he was enjoying, every night, you know, the different people that were playing to him. The money -- the bread was good, you know.
So it wound up that when he got home -- he didn't find out until later -- when he got home, he talked to his

wife, and he said, 'You were out that night.' She says, well, she began to get disgusted with him because he came back and told the guys this. She said, 'What number did you call,' and he called, She said, 'Well, that's not our number. You called the wrong number.'

Then he felt like two cents. He's ready to go out on the road, and he did. But, man, then Hawk and them told him -- they were playing this joke, said, 'We initiate anybody new that comes in, but it's all in good faith.' And they got to be the best of friends.
Then Red wound up pulling this on --
So this -- these are the things that happened, so that's one story on Red, but he was a great guy.
